      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> (Coronavirus Disease 2019)</content>

      <content name="altTitle">Coronavirus</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> (coronavirus disease 2019) is an illness caused by a virus. This virus is a coronavirus called SARS-CoV-2. It spreads when a person who has the infection breathes out droplets and very small particles that contain the virus. On this page, you'll find links to resources on important issues such as symptoms, risks, and how you can protect yourself and your family.</p><p>We also have pages on:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> testing</li><li><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> vaccines</li><li>Post-COVID conditions (long COVID)</li></ul></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> Testing</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> Antibody Test</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> Viral Test</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SARS-CoV-2 Testing</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> (coronavirus disease 2019) is a disease caused by a virus called SARS-CoV-2. There are two types of tests for this virus:</p><ul><li>A viral test tells you if you have a current infection. Viral tests can either be rapid tests or laboratory tests:
 <ul><li>Rapid tests can be done in minutes. They are often antigen tests, which look for specific proteins from the virus. Some rapid tests are self-tests which you can do at home.</li><li>Laboratory tests can take days to complete and include PCR tests.</li></ul>
</li><li>An antibody (serology) test might tell you if you had a past infection.</li></ul><p>If you need a <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> test, you can:</p><ul><li>Buy a self-test online or at a store. Make sure that the test you buy has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).</li><li>Check your state or local health department's website for information on testing in your area.</li><li>Contact your health care provider.</li></ul><p>Even if your <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> viral test is negative (the test did not detect the virus), you should still take steps to protect yourself and others.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/covid19vaccines.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> Vaccines</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>  (coronavirus disease 2019) is an illness caused by a virus. This virus is a coronavirus called SARS-CoV-2. Most people with <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> have mild symptoms, but some people become very sick. You can protect yourself by getting a <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> vaccine. The vaccines might help keep you from getting sick from <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>. And if you do get sick, the vaccines can reduce your risk for:</p><p></p><ul><li>Needing to go to urgent care or the emergency room</li><li>Getting severe illness </li><li>Being hospitalized </li><li>Dying</li><li>Getting long COVID </li></ul><p></p><p>It's important to stay up to date with the <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> vaccines. Contact your health care provider if you don't know when you need another vaccine or if you have other questions about the vaccines.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/longcovid.html">
      <content name="title">Long COVID</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Post-COVID Conditions</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Chronic COVID</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Long-haul COVID</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Long-term effects of COVID</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Post-acute <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC)</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is long COVID?<p><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> (coronavirus disease 2019) is an illness caused by a virus. Many people get better within a few days or weeks after being infected with the virus. But if you have symptoms that last for at least three months or more, you may have long COVID. Long COVID is a chronic (long-lasting) condition. It includes a wide range of symptoms or conditions that can range from mild to severe. You may:</p><ul><li>Have symptoms that linger for weeks, months, or even years</li><li>Seem to recover from <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> but then see your symptoms return</li><li>Develop new symptoms or new health conditions within a few months of having <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span></li></ul><p>There are several other names for long COVID. It can also be called post-COVID conditions, long-haul COVID, and post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC).</p>Who is more likely to develop long COVID?<p>Anyone who had <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>, whether it was severe or mild, can have long-lasting symptoms. But you are at higher risk of long COVID if you:</p><ul><li>Are female.</li><li>Are Hispanic or Latino.</li><li>Had severe <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> illness, especially if you were hospitalized or needed intensive care.</li><li>Had other health conditions before you got <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>.</li><li>Did not get a <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> vaccine.</li><li>Had multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS) during or after <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>. MIS is a rare but serious condition in which different parts of your body become inflamed.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of long COVID?<p>Long COVID does not affect everyone the same way. It can cause various types and combinations of symptoms in different people. The symptoms may affect different parts of the body, for example, you could have:</p><ul><li>General symptoms, such as fatigue and fever</li><li>Respiratory symptoms, such as trouble breathing and cough</li><li>Heart symptoms, such as chest pain and palpitations</li><li>Neurologic symptoms such as trouble thinking and concentrating ("brain fog"), headaches, and sleep problems</li><li>Digestive symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation, and stomach pain</li></ul><p>Some people may have a wide variety of symptoms that are similar to those of other conditions, such as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).</p><p>Most people's symptoms slowly improve over time. But for some people, the symptoms can last weeks, months, or longer. Sometimes the symptoms are severe enough to result in disability, including in children.</p><p>When long COVID affects multiple organs in your body, you may be at higher risk of developing other conditions. These include diabetes, heart diseases, and neurologic conditions.</p>How is long COVID diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for long COVID. To find out if you have long COVID, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history. This includes asking if you have had a diagnosis of <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>, either based on a positive test, symptoms, or exposure.</li><li>Will do a physical exam.</li><li>May order blood and imaging tests.</li></ul><p>Some of the symptoms of long COVID may be hard to explain. The results of blood and imaging tests may be normal. And people who have unexplained symptoms may sometimes be misunderstood by their providers. So, it can take some time to get a diagnosis.</p>What are the treatments for long COVID?<p>There is no specific treatment for long COVID. You and your provider can work together to create a personal care plan to help manage your symptoms and improve your quality of life.</p>Can long COVID be prevented?<p>The best way to prevent long COVID is to avoid getting <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>. Staying up to date with vaccines(including boosters) against <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> can help prevent <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> infection and protect against severe illness.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/commoncold.html">
      <content name="title">Common Cold</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cold, Common</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is the common cold?<p>The common cold is a mild infection of your upper respiratory tract (which includes your nose and throat). Colds are probably the most common illness. Adults have an average of 2-3 colds per year, and children have even more. Colds are more common in the winter and spring, but you can get them at any time.</p>What causes the common cold?<p>More than 200 different viruses can cause a cold, but rhinoviruses are the most common type. The viruses that cause colds are very contagious. They can spread from person to person through the air and close personal contact. You can also get infected when you touch something that has the virus on it and then touch your eyes, mouth, or nose. For example, you could get a cold after you shake hands with someone who has a cold or touch a doorknob that has the germs on it, and then touch your face.</p>What are the symptoms of the common cold?<p>The symptoms of a common cold usually include:</p><ul><li>Sneezing</li><li>Stuffy nose (congestion)</li><li>Runny nose</li><li>Sore throat</li><li>Coughing</li><li>Headache</li></ul><p>The symptoms usually start a few days after you become infected with the virus. Some symptoms can last for 10-14 days.</p>What are the treatments for the common cold?<p>There is no cure for the common cold. But there are treatments that can make you feel better while you wait for the cold to go away on its own:</p><ul><li>Getting lots of rest.</li><li>Drinking plenty of fluids.</li><li>Using a clean humidifier or cool mist vaporizer.</li><li>Gargling with warm salt water.</li><li>Using saline nose drops or sprays.</li><li>Taking over-the-counter pain or cold and cough medicines. But you need to be careful with certain medicines:
	<ul><li>Children and teens should not take aspirin.</li><li>Some cold and cough medicines contain ingredients that are not recommended for children. Talk with your child's health care provider before giving your child any cold and cough medicines.</li><li>Some cold and cough medicines contain pain relievers. If you also take a separate pain reliever with these medicines, you could be getting a dangerous amount of the pain reliever. Read the labels on the medicines and follow the instructions carefully. If you have questions, ask your provider or a pharmacist.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Antibiotics will not help with a cold. Antibiotics help with bacterial infections, not with viral infections such as colds.</p><p>Most people who have a cold will feel better after a week or two. However, some people who get a cold may develop other illnesses, such as bronchitis or pneumonia. This is more common in people with weakened immune systems, asthma, or other respiratory conditions. Contact your provider if you or your child have symptoms that concern you, such as:</p><ul><li>Trouble breathing or fast breathing</li><li>Dehydration</li><li>Fever that lasts longer than 4 days</li><li>Symptoms that last more than 10 days without improvement</li><li>Symptoms, such as fever or cough, that improve but then return or worsen</li><li>Worsening of chronic medical conditions</li></ul>Can the common cold be prevented?<p>There is no vaccine to protect against the common cold. But you may be able to reduce your risk of getting or spreading a cold by:</p><ul><li>Washing your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.</li><li>Avoiding touching your face, nose, or mouth with unwashed hands.</li><li>Avoiding close contact, such as kissing, shaking hands, and sharing cups and eating utensils, with others if you are sick or they are sick.</li><li>Cleaning and disinfecting surfaces that you frequently touch.</li><li>Covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue. Then throw away the tissue and wash your hands.</li><li>Staying home when sick.</li></ul><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>
